prompt: Why does this course show its programs in one language rather than in all four of the backend track?

choices.text: Because the patterns only exist in Python
choices.why: A strategy or an aggregate is the same idea in every language; the course says so in its first reading section.

choices.text: Four versions would bury the design under syntax, and pseudocode runs nowhere
choices.why: Right. One runnable language was the option left once the other two were weighed.

choices.text: Because Go and Java cannot express polymorphism
choices.why: Both can, through interfaces; the table in the section shows how each one writes it.

choices.text: Because the platform runs Python programs for the student
choices.why: The platform runs nothing; every program runs on your own machine.

prompt: Match the Python construct to what Java calls it.
What does the lab for this course need on your machine?

choices.text: Python, a database server and a web framework
choices.why: No lesson uses a server; lesson 10 uses SQLite, which comes inside Python.

choices.text: Python 3.12+, a terminal and an editor
choices.why: Right. Nothing outside the standard library, in any lesson.

choices.text: A virtual machine the platform provides
choices.why: The platform provides no machine; the lab is yours.

choices.text: Python plus the four languages of the backend track
choices.why: Your own language is welcome for rewriting the programs, and not needed to run them.

prompt: Your work laptop does not let you install software. Which path does the lab section point you to?

choices.text: Install Python anyway, with administrator rights borrowed from IT
choices.why: The section does not suggest working round your employer; it names the paths that need no install.

choices.text: Skip the lab and read the transcripts
choices.why: Every lesson asks you to run its programs; reading alone is the thing the lab exists to avoid.

choices.text: A virtual machine, or an online environment if that is not possible either
choices.why: Right. The VM is the choice for a computer that is not yours to install on, and online costs the computer nothing.

prompt: On Ubuntu 24.04, the command that runs Python is ___ .
Why does each lesson keep its programs in its own directory under ~/patterns?

choices.text: So two lessons never overwrite each other's files
choices.why: Right. Several lessons have a main.py or a test file of the same name.

choices.text: Because Python refuses to run a file outside a directory called patterns
choices.why: Python runs a file from anywhere; the directory is an arrangement for you.

choices.text: So the platform can collect them at the end of each lesson
choices.why: Nothing is collected; your programs stay on your machine.

prompt: Python answers can't open file '/home/ana/check.py'. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The file has an indentation error
choices.why: An indentation error is reported from inside the file; this one never opened it.

choices.text: The terminal is in the home directory, not in ~/patterns/oo
choices.why: Right. The path in the message shows where Python looked.

choices.text: The Python installed on this machine is older than the 3.12 the course needs
choices.why: An old Python would open the file and refuse later, with check.py's own sentence.

choices.text: The file was saved with Windows line endings
choices.why: Line endings do not stop a file being found; the message is about the path.

prompt: A traceback ends in ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'notices'. What fixes it?

choices.text: Installing notices from the internet with pip
choices.why: notices.py is a file from the lesson, not a published package.

choices.text: Renaming member.py to notices.py, so the import finds a file of that name
choices.why: Then member.py would be gone, and the import would find a file without the classes it needs.

choices.text: Saving notices.py in the same directory as member.py
choices.why: Right. Python looks first in the directory of the program it runs.

prompt: Put the steps for reading a Python error in the order the section gives them.
items: Read the last line: the kind of error and its message
Find the file and line number just above it
Compare that line with the lesson's, character by character
Check the line before it for a missing colon or bracket
trap: Starting from the top of a traceback reads the route before the cause.

prompt: What is encapsulation for, in the sense this lesson uses?

choices.text: Hiding the fields so other programmers cannot read the code
choices.why: The code stays readable; what is protected is the state, from being set to something the rules forbid.

choices.text: Keeping state and the rules about it together, so nothing outside breaks the rules
choices.why: Right. Private fields are one mechanism; the promise is the idea.

choices.text: Giving every field a getter and a setter
choices.why: That has the syntax and none of the promise: every rule is still kept by whoever calls the setters.

choices.text: Making the program run faster by caching values
choices.why: Speed is not the point; the fine in loan.py is computed every time on purpose.

prompt: A loan of 14 days starts on 2 March 2026. The fine is 50 cents a day. The book comes back on 21 March. What is the fine, in cents?
Why does Loan compute the fine every time instead of storing it in a field?

choices.text: Python cannot store an integer in an object's field
choices.why: It can; _due and _returned_on are fields.

choices.text: A stored fine would be faster, and the lesson wants to show the slow way first
choices.why: The lesson does not come back to a faster version; computing it is the design.

choices.text: A stored fine is a second copy of the dates, and copies drift apart
choices.why: Right. One source of truth, and the fine follows from it.

prompt: Some code writes loan._returned_on = None directly. What does Python do?

choices.text: Lets it: the underscore is a convention, not a lock
choices.why: Right. The line is for readers and reviewers; the interpreter does not enforce it.

choices.text: Raises AttributeError, because the field is private
choices.why: That is closer to Java or TypeScript's #field; Python has no private keyword.

choices.text: Refuses to run the file at all
choices.why: Nothing about the underscore is checked before running.

choices.text: Calls give_back automatically to keep the rules
choices.why: Assignment never calls a method on its own here; the write bypasses the rule entirely.

prompt: In items.py, what does Film's describe() do with super().describe()?

choices.text: Ignores it and writes a description from nothing
choices.why: That is what ReferenceBook does.

choices.text: Takes the parent's description and adds the running time to it
choices.why: Right. It extends rather than replaces.

choices.text: Calls Book's version of describe, because Book is defined first in the file
choices.why: Book is a sibling, not a parent; super() follows Film's own chain.

prompt: A call to describe() on a Film. Put the places Python looks in order.
trap: The child is searched first; that is what lets it override.

prompt: Somebody adds a required argument, branch, to Item.__init__. Which classes in items.py break?

choices.text: Only Item, because the children have constructors of their own
choices.why: Only Film has one, and it calls super().__init__ with two arguments.

choices.text: Only Film, because it is the one that calls super().__init__
choices.why: Book and ReferenceBook use Item's constructor directly, so their callers break too.

choices.text: All three children, plus every line that creates one
choices.why: Right. The parent's constructor is part of every child's contract.

choices.text: None, as long as branch has no default value
choices.why: No default is exactly what makes it required, and every call without it fails.

prompt: A fourth channel, WhatsApp, is added to notices.py. What has to change in remind()?

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. remind() knows one method, deliver, and the new class has it.

choices.text: A new elif branch for the new channel
choices.why: That is the version without polymorphism the section starts from.

choices.text: Its type annotation, to list the new class
choices.why: The annotation says Channel, which the new class satisfies by having deliver.

prompt: Match each language to how it decides that Email is a Channel.

pairs.right: The class must declare implements Channel
Having the method is enough, checked at compile time
Nothing is checked until the call runs

prompt: Calling a method because an object has it, without checking its class, is called ___ typing.
With inheritance, a member class exists for every combination of status and channel. With 2 statuses and 4 channels, how many classes below Member?
Bia switches from e-mail to SMS. In member.py, what happens to her Member object?

choices.text: It is replaced by a new SmsMember object
choices.why: That is what inheritance would force. Here the same object keeps its identity.

choices.text: The same object, with another channel
choices.why: Right. Composition lets a part change at run time.

choices.text: Python raises an error, because channel was set in the constructor
choices.why: A field set in the constructor can be reassigned later; nothing here forbids it.

prompt: Match each sentence to the idea it describes.

pairs.left: A loan refuses a second return
Film is an Item with a shorter loan
remind() calls deliver on whatever it is given
A member holds the channel it is reached by

prompt: Which of these are signs that a design needs composition rather than another subclass? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Two independent things vary, and each combination would need a class
choices.why: Right. That is the multiplication the composition section counts.

choices.text: The part has to change while the object lives
choices.why: Right. A class is fixed when the object is made; a field is not.

choices.text: The child really is a kind of the parent and keeps all its promises
choices.why: That is the case where inheritance fits; lesson 2 says when.

choices.text: Saying it aloud gives "has a" rather than "is a"
choices.why: Right. A member has a channel; it is not one.

prompt: ReferenceBook inherits from Item but cannot be lent. Which later idea of the course is that a warning about?

choices.text: The singleton, because only one reference book exists
choices.why: Several reference books exist; the problem is a promise the child cannot keep.

choices.text: Liskov substitution: a child must keep the promises its parent makes
choices.why: Right. Lesson 3 comes back to exactly this class.

choices.text: Event sourcing, because the loans should be stored as events
choices.why: Storage is a different question; this one is about what a subclass promises.

choices.text: Dependency injection, because the loan length should be passed in from outside the class
choices.why: Passing the number in would not make a reading-room book lendable.
